questions.prompt: You press Ctrl-C while a script runs in your terminal. Which signal does the process receive?

choices.text: `SIGTERM`
`SIGKILL`
`SIGINT`
`SIGHUP`

questions.explanation: Ctrl-C sends `SIGINT`, 'interrupt from keyboard'. `SIGTERM` is the generic polite request to exit, sent by `kill <PID>`; `SIGKILL` (`kill -9`) can't be caught; and `SIGHUP` is sent when the controlling terminal goes away, which `nohup` protects against.

questions.prompt: You run `docker stop` on your `agent-api` container (a Linux container, default settings). What does its main process receive?

choices.text: `SIGTERM`, then `SIGKILL` if it's still running after 10 seconds
`SIGKILL` straight away, so the app has no chance to clean up
`SIGINT`, then `SIGTERM` if it's still running after 30 seconds
`SIGHUP`, which asks the process to reload, and it keeps running

questions.explanation: Docker sends `SIGTERM` (or the image's `STOPSIGNAL`) so the app can shut down cleanly, waits the grace period (10 seconds by default for Linux containers, changed with `--timeout`), then sends `SIGKILL`. An app that ignores `SIGTERM` is killed mid-request after 10 seconds. `docker kill` is the command that sends `SIGKILL` at once.

questions.prompt: Why should your agent API handle `SIGTERM`, and how is `SIGTERM` different from `SIGKILL`?

model_answer.summary: `SIGTERM` is a request to exit that a process can catch and use to shut down cleanly; `SIGKILL` can't be caught, blocked or ignored and ends the process at once, so handling `SIGTERM` is your only chance to clean up.
key_points: `SIGTERM` asks a process to exit gracefully, and the process can catch it with a handler
`SIGKILL` can't be caught, blocked or ignored, so the process gets no chance to clean up
On `SIGTERM` the API should stop taking new requests, finish or cancel in-flight ones, flush traces and logs, and close database connections
`docker stop` sends `SIGTERM` and then `SIGKILL` after a grace period (10 seconds by default), so cleanup must fit in that time

questions.explanation: Deploys, restarts and scale-downs all stop processes with `SIGTERM` first. An API that ignores it loses in-flight agent runs and unflushed traces when the `SIGKILL` arrives. `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` are the two signals a process can never handle.

questions.prompt: In bash you type `MODEL=haiku` on one line and `python run.py` on the next. Inside `run.py`, `os.environ.get("MODEL")` is `None`. Why?

choices.text: Python only reads environment variables that start with `PYTHON`
Variable names must be lowercase to be passed on
The variable is set, but a new terminal window must be opened first
`MODEL` is a shell variable that wasn't exported, so child processes don't get it

questions.explanation: Assigning `MODEL=haiku` creates a variable in the shell only. `export MODEL=haiku` marks it to be passed to commands the shell runs, which then inherit it. To set it for a single command, write `MODEL=haiku python run.py`.

questions.prompt: `echo $PATH` prints `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin`, and there is a `python` in both `/usr/local/bin` and `/usr/bin`. Which one runs when you type `python`?

choices.text: `/usr/bin/python`, because system directories always take priority over local ones
`/usr/local/bin/python`: `$PATH` is searched left to right, first match wins
Whichever of the two was modified most recently, as the newer copy wins
Neither: the shell reports the name as ambiguous and runs nothing

questions.explanation: `$PATH` is a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches, left to right, for a command name. The first match wins, here `/usr/local/bin/python`. `which python` shows which file will run. That is why activating a virtualenv works: it puts the venv's `bin` directory at the front of `$PATH`.

questions.prompt: `traces.jsonl` has one JSON object per line, each with a numeric `cost`. Which command prints the average cost per run?

choices.text: `jq -s 'map(.cost) | add / length' traces.jsonl`
`jq 'map(.cost) | add / length' traces.jsonl`
`jq '.cost | add / length' traces.jsonl`
`jq -r '.cost' traces.jsonl | jq 'length'`

questions.explanation: By default jq runs the filter once for each JSON value in the input, so without `-s` every line is handled on its own and there is no list to average. `-s` (`--slurp`) reads the whole input into one array; `map(.cost)` turns it into an array of numbers; `add` sums them and `length` counts them. `length` on a single number gives its absolute value, not a count.

choices.text: Prints the file with the replacements, leaving `config.yaml` unchanged
Replaces only the first `gpt-4o` in the whole file
Replaces every `gpt-4o` on every line and writes the result back to `config.yaml`
Replaces only the first `gpt-4o` on each line

questions.explanation: `s/pattern/replacement/` substitutes a match on each line; the `g` flag makes it replace every match on the line rather than only the first, and `-i` edits the file in place instead of printing to standard output. Without `g` you get the 'first on each line' behaviour. The pattern is a regular expression, so a `.` would match any character.

questions.prompt: Write a `jq` command that computes the average cost per run from your JSONL trace file, and explain each part. What happens if the file is empty?

model_answer.summary: `jq -s 'map(.cost) | add / length' traces.jsonl` slurps every line into one array, extracts the costs, and divides their sum by their count; an empty file needs a guard because `add` of an empty array is `null`.
key_points: JSONL has one JSON object per line, and jq normally runs the filter once per object
`-s` (`--slurp`) reads all the objects into a single array so one filter sees them all
`map(.cost)` turns the array of objects into an array of costs
`add` sums the array and `length` counts it, so `add / length` is the mean
For an empty file the array is empty and `add` returns `null`, so guard it, for example `if length == 0 then 0 else (map(.cost) | add / length) end`

questions.explanation: The key idea is the difference between a stream of values and one array: aggregates like sums and averages need the whole set, which is what `--slurp` gives you. `jq -s 'map(.cost) | add'` for the total and `length` for the run count are the same pattern.

questions.prompt: `ssh` won't use your key, and `ls -l ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` shows `-rw-r--r--`. What is the fix?

choices.text: `chmod +x ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`
`chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`
`chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`
`chmod 755 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`

questions.explanation: The ssh manual says a private key must be readable by you but not accessible by others, and `ssh` ignores a key file that others can access. `-rw-r--r--` (644) lets everyone read it. `chmod 600` leaves read and write for the owner only (`-rw-------`). Adding execute or keeping others' read bits doesn't help.

choices.text: `rwxr-xr-x`
`rwxrw-r--`
`rwxr-xr--`

questions.explanation: Each digit is the sum of read (4), write (2) and execute (1), for owner, group and others in that order. 7 = 4 + 2 + 1 is `rwx` for the owner, 5 = 4 + 1 is `r-x` for the group, and 4 is `r--` for others. `rwxr-xr-x` is 755, the common setting for scripts everyone may run.

questions.prompt: You need to deploy to a new server over SSH. Explain how key-based login works, how you set it up, and how you would copy files to the server.

model_answer.summary: Generate a key pair, put the public key on the server, and keep the private key readable only by you; ssh then proves you hold the private key without sending it, and `scp` or `rsync` copies files over the same connection.
key_points: Key-based auth uses public-key cryptography: the client proves it owns the private key without revealing it
Generate a key pair with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` and install the public key on the server with `ssh-copy-id`
The private key must not be accessible by others (for example `chmod 600`), or ssh ignores it
Copy files with `scp local_file host:path`; `rsync` also works and skips files that are already identical on the other side

questions.explanation: Keys beat passwords because nothing secret crosses the network and the server only stores a public key. The permission check is ssh protecting you from a key other users could read. For repeated deploys, `rsync` saves time by sending only what changed.
